title: Expected vs realized move
teaches: Read the move the options market prices for a report (the implied move, quick-read from the at-the-money straddle), measure the move that really happened, divide one by the other, and say who was right and what a move far bigger than priced means for a holder.

facts.quote: Implied Volatility is a measure of how much the marketplace expects the asset price to move based on the price of the option.
facts.claim: Implied volatility is how far the market expects the price to move, read from option prices.

facts.quote: Statistical (Historical) Volatility is a measure of actual asset price changes over a specific period.
facts.claim: Historical volatility measures how much the price actually changed over a past period.

facts.quote: Implied volatility has no direct correlation to actual past historical or statistical volatility; rather it is a measure of predicted future movement.
facts.claim: Implied volatility is a forecast of future movement, not a record of past movement.

facts.quote: Implied volatility tends to increase when there is uncertainty or anticipated news, while it tends to decrease in times of calm.
facts.claim: Implied volatility tends to rise ahead of uncertainty or expected news and to fall when things calm down.

facts.quote: A decrease in implied volatility by 5% may result in the option losing around: .15 X 5 = $.75 in value.
facts.claim: All else equal, a drop in implied volatility takes value out of an option.

facts.quote: Higher volatility estimates indicate greater expected fluctuations (in either direction) in underlying price levels. This expectation generally results in higher option premiums for puts and calls alike.
facts.claim: A higher expected swing, in either direction, generally makes both calls and puts cost more.

facts.quote: A long straddle is a combination of buying a call and buying a put, both with the same strike price and expiration.
facts.claim: A straddle is a call and a put bought together at the same strike and expiry.

facts.quote: This strategy breaks even if, at expiration, the stock price is either above or below the strike price by the amount of premium paid.
facts.claim: At expiry, a straddle buyer breaks even only when the stock ends the full premium away from the strike.

facts.quote: The maximum loss is limited to the two premiums paid. The worst that can happen is for the stock price to hold steady and implied volatility to decline.
facts.claim: The straddle buyer's worst case is a stock that sits still while implied volatility falls.

facts.quote: This strategy involves selling a call option and a put option with the same expiration and strike price. It generally profits if the stock price and volatility remain steady.
facts.claim: The straddle seller generally profits when the stock and volatility stay steady.

facts.quote: The maximum gain is limited to the premiums received at the outset.
facts.claim: The straddle seller's best case is keeping the premium collected.

facts.quote: Review how implied volatility reflects the market's expectation of future stock movement and why it often falls sharply after earnings or other major announcements.
facts.claim: Implied volatility reflects expected movement, and it often falls sharply after earnings.

facts.quote: See how an option can lose value even when the stock moves in your favor
facts.claim: An option can lose value through an earnings report even when the stock moves your way.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: A triggered stop becomes a market order, and the fill can be far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Also, if you place your order before or after normal trading hours, consider the possibility that news events or other factors might significantly impact the price of the security when the market opens again.
facts.claim: News that lands outside the session can move the price a lot by the time the market opens again.

facts.quote: However, if markets are volatile and stock prices are changing rapidly, your stop order may be executed at a price that's significantly different from your stop price.
facts.claim: In a fast market a stop can fill well away from the stop price.

facts.quote: Immediately ahead of an earnings release, short-dated options prices reflect the market expectations of how a stock is likely to react.
facts.claim: Right before a report, short-dated option prices show the reaction the market expects.

facts.quote: The simplest way to estimate the magnitude of the reaction is by comparing the straddle price to historic moves.
facts.claim: Compare the straddle price with the stock's past reactions to size up the expected move.

facts.quote: Note that options pricing generally does not imply the direction of a reaction
facts.claim: Option prices generally do not say which way the stock will react.

facts.quote: just how much the stock is expected to move in either direction.
facts.claim: Option prices say how far the stock may move, up or down.

facts.quote: converted into an expected move using a 2/3 rule of thumb to estimate the highest probability point.
facts.claim: Cboe's note turned the implied standard deviation into an expected move with a two-thirds rule of thumb: one of several conventions.

facts.quote: strategies like straddles and strangles can profit from a large price move in either direction, provided the underlying's price move surpasses the total premium paid for the position.
facts.claim: A straddle profits from a big move either way only if the move beats the total premium paid.

facts.quote: Single stock options heading into earnings often carry high implied volatility, which inflates the premium on both calls and puts.
facts.claim: Into earnings, single-stock options often carry high implied volatility, which makes calls and puts pricier.

facts.quote: A trader buying a straddle on an individual stock may find that even a significant move in the stock doesn't cover the elevated cost of the options.
facts.claim: Even a big earnings move may not cover the high cost of a straddle.

facts.quote: Example A stock is trading at $200 ahead of earnings and the options market is implying a move of around 8% in either direction.
facts.claim: Cboe's example: a $200 stock with options implying about an 8% move either way.

facts.quote: And option traders would frequently use the price of a straddle as the expected move of a stock post-earnings event.
facts.claim: Option traders often use the straddle price as the expected move after earnings.

facts.quote: once that events comes and goes, the stock either moves by the expected move or more or it doesn't.
facts.claim: After the event the stock may move about as much as expected, more, or less.

facts.quote: it's not a determinant or determined factor that you could use with 100 percent accuracy.
facts.claim: The expected move is an estimate; it is not exact.

facts.quote: Historical volatility (HV) • Uses actual pricing data over the specified period • Measure of realized volatility
facts.claim: Historical volatility is built from the prices that actually printed: it measures realized volatility.

facts.quote: Long Straddle: Cost: $369 Maximum Gain = Unlimited Maximum Loss = $369 Results: Value: $0.04 + $2.77 = $2.81 * 100 shares = $281 Gain/Loss = $2.81 - $3.69 = $0.88 * 100 = $(88)
facts.claim: In Fidelity's earnings example, a straddle bought for $3.69 was worth $2.81 after the report: a loss of $88 per straddle.

facts.quote: Short Straddle: Credit: $354 Maximum Gain = $354 Maximum Loss = Unlimited Results: Value: $0.05 + $2.99 = $3.04 * 100 shares = $304 Gain/Loss = $3.54 - $3.04 = $0.54 * 100 = $54
facts.claim: In the same example, the straddle seller collected $3.54, bought it back for $3.04 and made $54 per straddle.

facts.quote: Volatility on the Calls: IV Mid was 92.88% with Vega at $0.0193 IV Mid ended up at 49.69% Option Value Lost due to Volatility = 92.88% - 49.69% = 43.19% * $0.0193 = about $0.83
facts.claim: In that example, implied volatility on the calls fell from 92.88% to 49.69% after the report, costing each call about $0.83.

facts.claim: The MSFT example uses prices from July 22, 2020, hours before an after-the-close report.

facts.claim: Option prices signal the move the market expects after a report.

facts.quote: The simplest way to see that anticipated move is to look at the nearest term, at-money straddle.
facts.claim: The quickest read of the expected move is the nearest-expiry, at-the-money straddle.

facts.quote: The midpoint of those options, minus any intrinsic value, is a quick guide to the implied move of the stock.
facts.claim: The straddle's midpoint, less any intrinsic value, is a quick guide to the implied move.
MSFT's straddle priced a $9.48 move on a $209.58 stock: about 4.5%.

facts.claim: AMD options priced about 7%, and the stock was about 10% lower the next morning.

facts.quote: Neither stock was pricing in a directional move, so the fact that we have one up and one down is not unexpected.
facts.claim: The options priced no direction for either stock, so one up and one down was no surprise.

facts.quote: Yesterday we highlighted options market expectations for Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD)
facts.claim: The AMD and GOOGL expectations were written up the day before the October 30, 2024 post, ahead of their reports.

facts.claim: NVDA's three reports before August 2025 were on November 20, 2024, February 26, 2025 and May 28, 2025.

facts.quote: At-money, near-term options are implying a roughly 6% post-earnings move for NVDA. That is below the 7.39% average of the stock's past 6 post-earnings moves
facts.claim: In August 2025 NVDA options priced about 6%, below the 7.39% average of its last six reactions.

facts.quote: Meta's stock surged 20.3 per cent for the session, also recording its biggest one-day percentage increase in a year

facts.quote: For options traders, earnings periods can present opportunities, but the potential for large gap moves introduces greater risk.
facts.claim: Earnings bring the risk of large gap moves.

facts.quote: So the stock is at 162 and a half and I'm going to look at the at-the-money or as close to at-the-money 162 and a half call and put.
facts.claim: Fidelity's live example: a $162.50 stock and the 162.50 strike call and put.

facts.quote: So one day to go, 162 and a half put and call is approximately trading for eight dollars and let's call it 30 cents.

walkthroughs.title: What the options are pricing
steps: Right before a report, short-dated options price the size of the reaction. That's the implied move, also called the expected move.
It's a size, not a direction. Options generally price how far, not which way.
The quick read: the at-the-money straddle in the nearest expiry that covers the report. Call plus put, divided by the stock price.
Cboe's example: a $200 stock with options implying a move of about 8% either way.

walkthroughs.title: A real one: MSFT, July 2020
steps: MSFT, July 22, 2020, a few hours before its report. The stock is $209.58.
The straddle, less its intrinsic value, comes to $9.48. That's about 4.5% priced.
Other methods give somewhat different numbers. Treat any of them as an estimate, never a promise.
Behind the straddle's price sits implied volatility: the options market's measure of how much it expects the price to move.

walkthroughs.title: Implied vs realized
steps: After the report, measure what the stock actually did. That's the realized move.
Divide realized by implied. Near one is about as priced. Under one is smaller, over one is bigger.
GOOGL once priced about 6%, and the next morning it was up just under that. About as priced.
The straddle price is the hurdle. Clear it at expiry and the buyers win. Fall short and the sellers do.

questions.q: Before a report, what does the stock's implied move tell you?
choices: How far options price it to move
Which way it is most likely to move
How far it moved after its last report
Where analysts expect the price to go
questions.answer: How far options price it to move
questions.why: How far options price it to move. The implied move is the size of the reaction the options market expects. Right before a report, short-dated option prices show it, Cboe says. OIC defines implied volatility as how much the market expects the price to move, read from option prices. It is not a direction. It is not last quarter's reaction, and it is not an analyst's price target.
questions.lesson_line: The implied move is the options market's estimate of the reaction's size.

wrong.Which way it is most likely to move: Options price a size, not a side. Up or down looks the same to the implied move.
wrong.How far it moved after its last report: That's history. You compare it with the implied move, but it isn't the implied move.
wrong.Where analysts expect the price to go: The implied move isn't anyone's price target. It comes from option prices, as a size either way.

questions.simple: How far options price the stock to move, since option prices carry the market's guess of the reaction's size.

reasons: four agreeing facts, one Tier 1 (OIC f1)

questions.q: The implied move tells you which way the stock should go after the report.
questions.why: False. The implied move is a size, not a direction. Cboe notes that option pricing generally does not imply which way a stock will react. It shows how much it may move either way. OIC says the same: the result describes magnitude, not direction. It does not mean the stock will sit still either. It can move the full amount, up or down.
questions.lesson_line: The implied move is a size. It says nothing about up or down.
questions.simple: False, because option prices show how big a move may be, not which way the stock will go.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ move is how far the stock actually went after the report.
questions.why: Realized. The realized move is what the stock actually did after the report, measured from real prices. OIC calls historical volatility a measure of actual price changes, and Fidelity calls it realized volatility. The implied move is the forecast read from option prices before the report. Expected is another name for the implied move, not the realized one.
questions.lesson_line: Implied is the forecast. Realized is what the stock really did.
questions.simple: Realized is the move the stock really made after the report, while implied was the guess made before it.

questions.q: Which options give the quickest read of the implied move?
questions.why: The nearest at-the-money straddle. Use the nearest expiry that covers the report and the strike nearest the stock price, then add the call and the put. Sosnick at Interactive Brokers calls this the simplest way to see the anticipated move. Fidelity says traders often use the straddle price as the expected move. Sosnick also takes out any intrinsic value, and Cboe's note used a different method. Treat the result as a quick read, not an exact number.
questions.lesson_line: Nearest expiry, strike nearest the price, call plus put. That's your quick read.

wrong.Far out-of-the-money calls: Those only pay on a big move up. The at-the-money straddle prices a move either way.
wrong.The longest-dated puts: Long-dated options mix in months of other risk. You want the nearest expiry that covers the report.
wrong.The call with most volume: Volume shows activity, not the priced move. Read the at-the-money straddle.

questions.simple: The nearest at-the-money straddle, because a call plus a put at the strike nearest the price shows the move priced.

reasons: fixed before (expiry that covers the report)
key rests on two Tier 2 publishers plus Cboe

questions.q: A straddle buyer makes money at expiry as long as the stock moves.
questions.why: False. A straddle buyer owns a call and a put at one strike. OIC says it only breaks even at expiry when the stock ends the full premium above or below the strike. A smaller move, either way, loses money. The most the buyer can lose is the two premiums paid.
questions.lesson_line: The straddle price is the hurdle. The move has to clear it.
questions.simple: False, because at expiry the stock must move more than the full price paid for the straddle before the buyer makes money.

questions.q: Implied volatility tends to rise ahead of known news like an earnings report.
questions.why: True. OIC says implied volatility tends to increase when there is uncertainty or anticipated news, and to decrease in calm times. Cboe adds that single-stock options heading into earnings often carry high implied volatility, which inflates the premium on calls and puts. The word tends matters: it is a pattern, not a rule. And it often falls sharply after the report.
questions.lesson_line: Into the report, options tend to get pricier. That's the market paying up for the unknown.
questions.simple: True, because implied volatility tends to rise when news like an earnings report is coming.

reasons: fixed before (hedge added to lesson line)

questions.q: The report is out. What usually happens to implied volatility on the near-term options?
questions.why: It often falls sharply. Once the news is out, much of the uncertainty that was priced in is gone.
questions.lesson_line: The report removes the unknown. Implied volatility usually comes down with it.

wrong.It usually doubles: Rising is the build-up before the report. After it, implied volatility tends to drop.
wrong.It holds until expiry: It moves with supply and demand all the time. After a report it often falls right away.
wrong.It follows the stock's direction: Implied volatility measures expected size, not direction. It can fall after a big move up or down.

questions.q: Fill the blank with the right word.
questions.sentence: A straddle seller can make at most the ___ collected.
questions.why: Premium. OIC says the straddle seller's maximum gain is limited to the premiums received at the outset. The seller generally profits when the stock and volatility stay steady. A move past the premium, either way, is a loss for the seller instead. The strike is where the move is measured from, not what the seller keeps.
questions.lesson_line: The seller's best case is keeping the premium. The buyer's hurdle is that same premium.
questions.simple: Premium, because the most a straddle seller can make is the premium collected up front.

questions.q: The stock is $80. The $80 call and put in the nearest expiry cost $4.40 together. What move, in percent, is priced?
questions.why: 5.5%. Divide the straddle price by the stock price: $4.40 divided by $80 is 5.5%. The strike equals the stock price, so neither option has intrinsic value. That makes the full-straddle read and the read that subtracts intrinsic value give the same answer. It is an estimate of the move's size, either way, not a promise or a limit.
questions.lesson_line: Straddle divided by price gives the implied move in percent. It's an estimate, not a promise.
questions.simple: About 5.5%, because $4.40 for the straddle divided by the $80 stock price gives the move options price.

reasons: fixed before (strike set to the stock price)

wrong.18.2%: You flipped it and divided the stock price by the straddle.
wrong.2.8%: You used about half the straddle, only one leg.
wrong.55%: A decimal slip: you moved the point one place.

questions.q: A stock's last close before its report was $80. Its first close after was $86.80. What was the realized move, in percent?
questions.why: 8.5%. The realized move is how far the stock really moved because of the report. Find it on a daily chart. Take the last close before the report and the first close after it. The rise is $86.80 minus $80, which is $6.80. Divide that by the starting $80 and you get 8.5%. Close to close catches the whole gap, because news lands while the market is shut. The implied move is the forecast read from options before the report. Realized is what printed. Set the two side by side to see if the stock moved more or less than priced.
questions.lesson_line: Realized move = (close after minus close before) divided by close before. Then hold it up against the implied move.
questions.simple: It was 8.5%, the gain from the last close before the report to the first close after, divided by the $80 start.

wrong.7.8%: You divided the $6.80 rise by the new $86.80 close. Always divide by where the move started, the old $80 close.
wrong.6.8%: That is the rise in dollars, $6.80, read as a percent. Divide it by the $80 start to turn it into a percent.
wrong.108.5%: That is the new close as a share of the old one. The move is only the part above the start, so subtract the starting $80 first.

deeper.example: A real one: before AMD's report, options priced about 7%. The next morning the stock was trading about 10% lower. That is bigger than priced, so the options likely priced too small a move.

questions.q: HXLR closed at $50 before earnings. Its at-the-money straddle cost $2. It closed at $55 after. Realized move divided by implied move?
questions.why: 2.5x. A straddle is a call and a put at the same strike, and its price is the quick read of the move options price. $2 divided by the $50 stock is 4%. The stock went from $50 to $55, which is a 10% move. Realized divided by implied is 10 divided by 4, which is 2.5. Under one means smaller than priced. Over one means bigger. OIC says options are sometimes called outperforming expectations when the stock moves more than implied. At 2.5 the stock moved far more than options priced. To work it out by hand, divide the nearest at-the-money straddle price by the stock price.
questions.lesson_line: Straddle over price gives the priced move. Realized over implied tells you how it compared.
questions.simple: It is 2.5, because the stock moved two and a half times what the straddle priced.

reasons: fixed before (OIC f53 and f54 added)

wrong.6.0x: You subtracted the 4% from the 10% instead of dividing.
wrong.14.0x: You added the 4% and the 10% instead of dividing.
wrong.0.4x: You flipped it and divided the priced 4% by the realized 10%. Put the realized move on top.

questions.q: The implied move is the most a stock can move after the report.
questions.why: False. The implied move is an estimate of size, not a limit. Fidelity's presenter says the stock then moves by the expected move, or more, or it doesn't. It is not accurate 100 percent of the time. AMD options once priced about 7%, and the next morning the stock was about 10% lower. Treat it as a guide, not a ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: The implied move is a guide, not a ceiling. The real move can be bigger.
questions.simple: False, because the implied move is only an estimate, and a stock can move well past it.

reasons: Fidelity and IBKR agree (two Tier 2 publishers)

questions.story: Options price a 5% move into the report. The stock gaps 12% and holds there into expiry.
questions.q: On the at-the-money straddle, who came out ahead?
questions.why: The buyers of the straddle. At expiry a straddle buyer breaks even when the stock ends the full premium away from the strike, either way, OIC says. Options priced about 5% and the stock held 12% away, so the straddle is worth far more than it cost. A move this far past the premium is a loss for the sellers. Falling implied volatility can shave value before expiry, but at expiry only the move counts.
questions.lesson_line: A move past the straddle price by expiry pays the buyers. A smaller one pays the sellers.

wrong.The sellers of the straddle: Sellers do well when the move stays inside the premium. A move far past it costs them.
wrong.Neither side, it's about even: Even would need the move to land right at the premium paid. It went well past it.
wrong.Depends on implied volatility: Falling volatility hurts buyers before expiry. At expiry only the move counts, and 12% is far past the 5% priced.

questions.simple: The buyers won, because the stock moved 12% and held there, far past the 5% move the straddle priced.

questions.story: From a Fidelity options webinar: before a report, the at-the-money straddle cost $3.69. After the report it was worth $2.81.
questions.q: Who came out ahead on that straddle?
choices: No way to tell without the move
questions.why: The seller of the straddle. It cost $3.69 before the report and was worth $2.81 after, so whoever bought it lost and whoever sold it gained. In Fidelity's example the buyer lost $88 on one straddle and the seller made $54. Whatever the stock did, it was not enough to cover what was paid. Cboe warns that even a big earnings move may not cover the high cost of the options.
questions.lesson_line: A stock can move and the straddle still lose. The move has to beat what was paid.

wrong.Both, since the stock moved: A move smaller than the premium hands the win to the seller. The buyer lost.
wrong.The buyer of the straddle: The straddle was worth less after the report than it cost. That's a loss for the buyer.
wrong.No way to tell without the move: The straddle's own prices settle it. It cost $3.69 and was worth $2.81 after, so the buyer lost and the seller gained.

questions.simple: The seller came out ahead, because the straddle was worth less after the report than the buyer paid for it.

deeper.example: Fidelity's numbers: after the report the call was worth $0.04 and the put $2.77, $2.81 in all. Against $3.69 paid, that is $0.88 a share, or $88 on one straddle of 100 shares. The seller's prices were different: the seller collected $3.54 and paid $3.04 to close, a $54 gain. The two sides do not mirror exactly, but the verdict is the same.

questions.q: NVDA, August 2025: options priced about 6%. Its last six reactions averaged 7.39%. What does that tell you?
choices: Options priced a smaller move than usual
Options priced a bigger move than usual
The stock likely rises on the report
The options are mispriced and too cheap
questions.answer: Options priced a smaller move than usual
questions.why: Options priced a smaller move than usual. In August 2025, NVDA's at-the-money near-term options implied about 6%, below the 7.39% average of its past six post-earnings moves, Sosnick wrote. That says the market expected a calmer reaction than its history, nothing more. It gives no direction. Below average alone does not show mispricing. Cboe found the big tech options it studied generally priced moves slightly below their historical averages.
questions.lesson_line: Hold the implied move up against the stock's past reactions. That tells you if options expect a big one.

wrong.Options priced a bigger move than usual: 6% is below the 7.39% average, so it's smaller, not bigger.
wrong.The stock likely rises on the report: The implied move has no direction. It can't tell you up or down.
wrong.The options are mispriced and too cheap: Below average alone doesn't make them wrong. Cboe found big tech options generally price moves slightly below their history.

questions.simple: Options priced a smaller move than usual, because about 6% is below the 7.39% average of its last six reactions.

reasons: fixed before (Cboe f56 and OIC f52 added)

questions.q: After a report, implied volatility on the calls fell from 92.88% to 49.69%. All else equal, what did that do to the calls?
questions.why: Took value out of them. All else equal, lower implied volatility means a lower premium. OIC's own example shows an option losing value when implied volatility drops. In Fidelity's example, the fall from 92.88% to 49.69% cost each call about $0.83. Higher volatility lifts puts and calls alike, so a fall cuts both. It happens even if the stock holds still.
questions.lesson_line: After a report, the volatility you paid for often drains out. That's the volatility crush.

wrong.Added value to them: That's what rising implied volatility does. A fall does the opposite.
wrong.Nothing, the stock decides: Implied volatility is part of an option's price. All else equal, a drop like this cuts the premium even if the stock holds still.
wrong.Shifted value to the puts: Implied volatility has no side. OIC: higher volatility raises puts and calls alike, so a fall cuts both.

questions.simple: It took value out of the calls, because lower implied volatility makes options cheaper even when nothing else changes.

deeper.trap: The trap is buying calls into a report because you are sure the stock will rise. Even if it does, the drop in implied volatility after the news can eat the gain. OIC shows how an option can lose value even when the stock moves in your favor.

reasons: fixed before (hedge added to lesson line)

questions.story: NVDA reported on May 28, 2025. Options priced about a 7% move. The stock rose 3.25%.
questions.q: What is the realized move divided by the implied move, and what does it say?
questions.why: About 0.46x, smaller than priced. Divide the realized move by the implied move: 3.25 divided by 7 is about 0.46. Options priced about 7% for NVDA's May 28, 2025 report, and the stock rose 3.25%, Sosnick wrote. Under one means a smaller move than priced. OIC says the options are then sometimes called underperforming expectations. The rise itself is not the point: options price size, not direction.
questions.lesson_line: A reaction well under the priced move tells you something too. The market braced for more than it got.

wrong.About 1x, right on the price: Right on would need a move near 7%. The stock moved 3.25%.
wrong.About 2.15x, bigger than priced: That divides the wrong way: 7 over 3.25. Put the realized move on top: 3.25 over 7.
wrong.About 0.54x, smaller than priced: That's the shortfall, 7 minus 3.25, over 7. The ratio is 3.25 divided by 7, about 0.46.

questions.simple: About 0.46x, because the 3.25% rise was less than half of the 7% move options priced.

deeper.trap: Two traps. Dividing the wrong way turns a move under half the priced one into one that looks twice as big. Subtracting first gives the shortfall, not the ratio. Put the realized move on top and divide. Under one is smaller than priced, over one is bigger.

questions.story: NVDA reported on February 26, 2025. Options priced about an 8.4% move. The stock fell 8.48%.
questions.q: Did options get the reaction right?
choices: Yes, the size was about as priced
No, it went down instead of up
No, a drop that big is a shock
Yes, they priced a drop of 8.4%
questions.answer: Yes, the size was about as priced
questions.why: Yes, the size was about as priced. Options priced about 8.4% for NVDA's February 2025 report, and the stock fell 8.48%, Sosnick wrote. That is almost exactly the expected size. Direction was never part of the price: Cboe and OIC both say option prices describe how big, not which way. A big drop that matches the priced move is the market getting it right.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the implied move on size. A big drop that matches the priced move is the market getting it right.

wrong.No, it went down instead of up: Options didn't price a direction. A fall of the priced size is right on.
wrong.No, a drop that big is a shock: Big is relative. Options priced about 8.4%, and the stock fell 8.48%. That is the priced size.
wrong.Yes, they priced a drop of 8.4%: Options priced about 8.4% either way, not a drop. They got the size right; a direction was never priced.

questions.simple: Yes, because the 8.48% drop was almost exactly the 8.4% move options priced, and options price size, not direction.

deeper.trap: The trap is grading options on direction. A trader who expected a rise calls this a miss. But the options priced only size: about 8.4% either way. A fall of 8.48% is the forecast working, and the same move up would be judged the same.

questions.q: Two websites can show different implied moves for the same report without either one being wrong.
questions.why: True. There is more than one method. Fidelity's presenter uses the full straddle price as the expected move. Sosnick at Interactive Brokers subtracts any intrinsic value from the straddle's midpoint. Cboe's note turned the implied standard deviation into an expected move with a 2/3 rule of thumb. Each is an estimate, so two sites can show different numbers for one report. Know which method your tool uses before you compare.
questions.lesson_line: Check how your tool works out the implied move before you compare numbers across sites.
questions.simple: True, because tools work out the implied move in different ways, so their numbers can differ and both be fair.

deeper.example: Sosnick's MSFT read, July 2020: the two 210 options cost 4.75 and 5.15, with the stock at 209.58. With the strike above the stock, the put had intrinsic value. He took it out and got $9.48, about 4.5%. Fidelity's full-straddle read would come out a little higher on the same options. Same options, two fair numbers.

reasons: three Tier 2 publishers show three methods

questions.story: AMD reported in late October 2024. Options priced about a 7% move. The next morning the stock was about 10% lower.
questions.q: How big was the reaction against what was priced?
questions.why: About 1.4x, bigger than priced. Divide the realized move by the implied move: about 10 divided by about 7 is about 1.4. AMD options priced about 7% for its late October 2024 report. The next morning the stock was about 10% lower, Sosnick wrote. Bigger than the market expected, but well short of twice. Sosnick's own read: the market wasn't too far off. Both figures are approximate, and the 10% was a morning price, not a close.
questions.lesson_line: Read the ratio, not the headline. Bigger than priced, but not a shock.

wrong.About 0.7x, smaller than priced: That flips the ratio. Divide the realized move by the implied move, not the other way round.
wrong.About 1x, right on the price: Right on would be close to 7%. About 10% is clearly bigger.
wrong.About -1.4x, opposite to priced: Options priced about 7% either way, with no direction. Use the size of the drop, not its sign.

questions.simple: About 1.4x, because a drop of about 10% is bigger than the 7% options priced, but well short of double.

deeper.trap: A headline that says a stock fell 10% sounds like options missed. Against about 7% priced it is about 1.4x: bigger than expected, not a shock. Check the basis too. Sosnick's 10% was a morning-after price, not the day's close, so the ratio could shift by the close.

questions.q: Meta, February 2024: front-week options implied about a 9% move. The stock closed up 20.3%. Realized divided by implied?
questions.why: 2.3. Divide 20.3 by 9: about 2.3. Before Meta's February 2024 report, its at-the-money front-week options had an implied volatility of about 9%, Sosnick wrote. The stock closed up 20.3% for the session, Reuters reported, its biggest one-day percentage gain in a year. More than double the priced move means the news landed far outside what the market expected.
questions.lesson_line: Twice the priced move or more means the news landed far outside what the market priced.
questions.simple: About 2.3, because Meta's 20.3% jump was more than twice the 9% move its options implied.

deeper.trap: Mixing bases. The 9% came from front-week implied volatility before the report. The 20.3% is Reuters' session close. Different methods and times can shift a ratio, so read it as about 2.3, not exact. More than double either way says the report landed far outside what options priced.

reasons: pairs two writers' figures (IBKR priced, Reuters close)

wrong.0.4x: You flipped it and divided the 9% by the 20.3%.
wrong.0.2x: A decimal slip: you moved the point one place.
wrong.1.3x: You divided the extra move past 9 by 9, not the whole move.

questions.story: You own a stock into its report, which lands after the close. Your stop sits 4% below. Options price about a 9% move.
questions.q: What can your stop do for you overnight?
choices: Little, the open can gap right past it
Fill at the stop price on any gap
questions.answer: Little, the open can gap right past it
questions.why: Little. News outside the session can move the price a lot by the open, and a triggered stop becomes a market order that can fill far below your stop. A gap bigger than 4% sits well inside the 9% options priced.
questions.lesson_line: If the priced move is bigger than your stop, the stop isn't your risk. The gap is.

wrong.Cap the loss at 4%: A stop is a trigger, not a price. If the stock opens 9% lower, the sale happens near there.
wrong.Fill at the stop price on any gap: A triggered stop is a market order. On a gap it fills at the market, which can be far from your stop.

questions.q: You bought 200 shares at $50 just before the report, stop 4% below. It opens 9% lower and the stop fills there. How much did you lose?
questions.why: $900. 200 shares times $50 times 9%. That's more than double the 4% you planned to risk.
questions.lesson_line: Holding through a report, size for a gap at least as big as the priced move, not just for your stop.

questions.q: A stock moves twice its implied move after the report. What does that tell you?
choices: The report surprised the options market
The options were priced too high
The move will reverse the next day
questions.answer: The report surprised the options market
questions.why: The report surprised the options market. Before a report, short-dated option prices show the reaction the market expects, Cboe says. A move twice that size went far past it. OIC has a name for a move bigger than implied: the options are sometimes said to be outperforming expectations. It does not predict the next day. And implied volatility often falls sharply after a report rather than rising. Note the surprise, then judge the chart on its own merits.
questions.lesson_line: Twice the priced move means the report caught the market off guard. Note it, then judge the chart on its own merits.

wrong.The options were priced too high: Backwards. The stock moved more than options priced, not less. Priced too high would show as a move that fell short.
wrong.The move will reverse the next day: Nothing in the implied move predicts tomorrow. Judge what happens next on its own.
wrong.Implied volatility will now rise: After a report, implied volatility often falls sharply. The event it was pricing is over.

questions.simple: The report surprised the options market, because the stock moved twice as far as options had priced for it.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the ratio as a forecast. Twice the priced move says the news surprised the market. It does not say the move will reverse or run on, or that options were too dear. Judge what comes next from the chart and your plan.

reasons: key text reworded to remove a longest-answer tell

questions.q: Under our rule, a trade up 2R is sold before the report, even if options price a small move.
questions.why: True. We hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R, and 2R is short of that. The size of the priced move does not change the rule. It is an estimate, and the stock can move more than priced.
questions.lesson_line: A small priced move is no reason to hold. We hold through a report only when up 5R.
questions.simple: True, because we hold through a report only when the trade is up 5R, whatever move options price.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a small implied move as a safe report. The stock can move by the expected move, or more. Our rule looks at your gain so far, not the forecast.

conflicts: How the implied move is computed differs by source. Fidelity's 2022 class uses the full at-the-money straddle price; Interactive Brokers (Sosnick) subtracts any intrinsic value from the straddle midpoint; Cboe's Mag 7 note converts the implied standard deviation with a 2/3 rule of thumb; third-party tools (not cited) use 85% of the straddle. Our own earnings card (api/services/earnings_enrichment.get_implied_move) uses the full straddle divided by spot. The file teaches the full straddle as 'the quick read', calls every figure 'about', and q19 keys that two tools can differ without either being wrong.

q21 (Meta, February 2024): Sosnick's 'implied volatility of about 9%' is the daily implied volatility of the front-week at-the-money options, which he treats as the priced move (his 2020 post: daily IV and the straddle 'generally agree if the options are very short-lived'). A straddle-based figure would likely be somewhat lower, which only raises the ratio; 'more than double' holds either way. The question says 'implied about a 9% move', not 'the straddle priced 9%'.

Realized-move basis differs by source. Reuters' 20.3% (Meta) is the session close. Sosnick's AMD 'currently about -10% lower' and GOOGL 'up by just under that amount' are intraday the morning after (post at 1:00 pm, October 30, 2024); q20 says 'the next morning' and uses no close. His NVDA figures (+3.25%, -8.48%) are 'post-earnings moves'; the post does not say open or close. Each ratio states its realized basis: q17, q18 and q20 use one writer's pair (Sosnick's priced move and his reported reaction); q21 pairs Sosnick's pre-report figure with Reuters' session close.

MSFT, July 2020 (s14) is used only to read the implied move (9.48 / 209.58, about 4.5%). Its realized move is left out on purpose: the 209.58 base is an intraday price hours before the report, not the prior close, so a ratio against the next day's close (202.54) would mix bases.

s13's straddle example (2016 slides) does not name the stock; an earlier slide in the deck says 'The earnings date on this example is 2/25/16', but the slides never tie that date to the trade slides, so q14 gives no ticker and no date.

Cboe's insights posts are filed Tier 2 although cboe.com is listed under Tier 1 exchanges: they are research commentary, not a rule. Every key that cites them also cites a Tier 1 fact or a second Tier 2 publisher.
q20 says 'reported in late October 2024': the IBKR post (s15) is dated October 30, 2024 and says the AMD and GOOGL expectations were written up 'yesterday'; it does not state the report date itself.
